paragraphs.heading: The blood-red stone
paragraphs.text: Hematite is an iron-oxide mineral. Its name comes from haima, the Greek word for blood, because some varieties of it are red. The English name reached us through Middle French and Latin from an Ancient Greek phrase meaning "blood-red stone".

paragraphs.heading: Where it forms
paragraphs.text: Large deposits of hematite sit in banded iron formations. Gray hematite typically turns up where water stands still or in mineral hot springs, such as the ones in Yellowstone National Park. The mineral may precipitate in the water and build up in layers on the bottom of the lake or spring. Hematite can also occur where there is no water, and then it is usually the result of volcanic activity. Clay-sized crystals of it may also form in soil through weathering.

paragraphs.heading: A colour people kept
paragraphs.text: The colour of hematite is often used as a pigment. Ochre is a clay coloured by hematite, which can make up anywhere from 20% to 70% of it. Red ochre holds unhydrated hematite, and yellow ochre holds hydrated hematite (Fe₂O₃ · H₂O). The main use of ochre is tinting things with a colour that lasts.

paragraphs.heading: One of the oldest materials
paragraphs.text: Writing, drawing and decorating with the red chalk of this mineral is among the earliest such uses in human history. The earliest known human use of the powdery mineral so far dates to 164,000 years ago, by people living in the Pinnacle Point caves in what is now South Africa, possibly for social purposes. Hematite residues also turn up in graves from 80,000 years ago. Red chalk mines from 5000 BC have been found near Rydno in Poland and Lovas in Hungary. On the island of Elba, rich deposits have been mined since the time of the Etruscans.

paragraphs.heading: Barely magnetic
paragraphs.text: Hematite responds only very feebly to a magnetic field. Unlike magnetite, it is not noticeably pulled toward an ordinary magnet. Its magnetic structure was a matter of much discussion and debate during the 1950s. The magnetic properties of hematite in bulk also differ from those of hematite at the nanoscale, which means super small.

paragraphs.heading: Mines and their leftovers
paragraphs.text: Underground hematite mining is classified as a cancer hazard to humans. Hematite is also present in tailings, the waste of iron mines. A recently developed process called magnetation uses magnets to pick waste hematite out of old mine tailings in the Mesabi Range iron district of Minnesota. Falu red, a pigment used in traditional Swedish house paints, is made from the tailings of the Falun Mine.

paragraphs.heading: Hematite on Mars
paragraphs.text: Hematite has been seen on Mars. Its spectral signature was picked up by the infrared spectrometer on two NASA spacecraft orbiting the planet, Mars Global Surveyor and 2001 Mars Odyssey. The mineral was abundant at two sites. One is Terra Meridiani, near the Martian equator at 0° longitude, and the other is Aram Chaos, near the Valles Marineris. Several other sites showed hematite too, Aureum Chaos among them.
